newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mostly higher in U.S., sterling supreme. [CORRECTED 22:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mostly higher in U.S., sterling supreme. [CORRECTED 22:40 GMT]

text.p: The dollar closed higher in the U.S. against most currencies, but failed to halt the surging British pound, which powered to a 49-month high.
U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Jeffrey Shafer gave the dollar a lift late in U.S. trading by reiterating the Clinton administration supports a "strong" dollar.

That statement offset a Tuesday Treasury release that said Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin did not discuss currency rates during a phone call with Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, foreign exchange traders said.
Some analysts interpreted Tuesday's Treasury statement as a reversal of its oft-stated position on the dollar.

"Shafer is well aware of the impact of his statement. The United States and its trading partners are trying to manage the level of the dollar against the yen," said Paul Park, currency trader at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
The dollar ended higher at 111.70/80 yen, up from 111.40/45 at the open, and 1.5074/79 marks from 1.5052/62.
Meanwhile, sterling closed higher at $1.6600/10 from $1.6532/37. The pound earlier hit $1.6628 and a 29-month high above 2.5000 marks.
(Corrects sterling rate from 1.2500 marks).
Investors flocked to the pound after a report showed unemployment in the United Kingdom fell to 7.2 percent, its lowest point in nearly six years.
A separate release showed Bank of England Governor Eddie George had warned against coming U.K. inflation at a monetary policy meeting on September 23.
Taken together, the reports suggested British officials will soon raise interest rates, even after they raised them on October 30, traders said.
Higher U.K. interest rates would aid the pound by boosting the relative returns of assets denominated in sterling.

"The hawkish statements from George reinforce the expectation that the U.K. rate hike two weeks ago is not enough and not the last," said Seth Garrett, director of foreign exchange at CS First Boston.
In the U.S., the Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee opted not to change short-term interest rates during a day-long meeting Wednesday.
Few, if any, market players expected a rate move at the meeting and the dollar failed to respond when the panel announced its decision during late U.S. trade.
The dollar drew some support against European currencies in overnight trading when two senior Bundesbank officials hinted that Germany might cut interest rates in the future.

Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler told a banking conference the recent German rate cut cycle had not necessarily ended, while a magazine article quoted fellow council member Olaf Sievert refusing to confirm the easing cycle was over.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2705/15 Swiss francs from 1.2667/77. The U.S. currency edged lower to Canadian $1.3337/42 from C$1.3343/48.
The Australian dollar rose to $0.7883/83 from $0.7875/80.
--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664
